domain: Constitutional Law / Political Philosophy / Speech Regulation
topic_summary: Analysis of the constitutional and philosophical debate over free speech protection boundaries. The First Amendment's scope is contested between near-absolute protection (protecting all ideas regardless of harm) and harm-limited approaches (permitting regulation when speech causes demonstrable injury). The disagreement centers on whether harm overrides protection and how to define actionable harm.

key_entities: U.S. Supreme Court (constitutional adjudicator; shifted toward absolutism 1960s-1970s)
Justice Hugo Black (absolutist advocate; literal reading of 'no law')
Justice William O. Douglas (absolutist advocate; shared Black's approach)
John Stuart Mill (harm principle theorist; 19th century philosopher)
Contemporary harm scholars (document tangible harms from bigoted speech)
Elon Musk (contemporary absolutist advocate in platform governance)
First Amendment (constitutional text; 'Congress shall make no law')
key_tensions: Literal text ('no law') vs contextual interpretation (harm exceptions)
Democratic self-governance value vs minority protection from systemic harm
Individual liberty maximization vs aggregate harm minimization
key_mechanisms: Strict scrutiny doctrine (heightens barrier to speech regulation)
Content/viewpoint discrimination test (presumptively invalidates content-based rules)
Categorical exclusions (obscenity, incitement, true threats carved out as 'unprotected')
key_absences: Enforcement mechanism for harm-limited approach (who measures harm, by what standard)
Exit option for minorities bearing disproportionate costs of absolutism

axiom_contradictions.basis: Absolutist axiom holds that 'no law' is categorical and harm is an impermissible basis for regulation; harm-limited axiom holds that demonstrable harm is the legitimate basis for regulation. No single framework can hold both: accepting harm as a valid regulatory basis requires rejecting categorical protection, and vice versa.
